We explore air-quality measurements from New York between May and September
1973, first as pairs of variables and then over time. We use **ggplot2** in R
and **seaborn/matplotlib** in Python. Choose a language in any tab to switch
all the tabs, and run the examples in order so that earlier objects are
available.

Keep the `data` folder beside this file. See
[First Steps with ggplot2](first-steps-with-ggplot2.html) for the building
blocks of a plot in both languages.

## Getting started

Install packages once, then load or import them in each new session. Python
uses pandas for tables, statsmodels for linear regression, and scikit-misc
for LOESS and its confidence intervals.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

If needed, run this once:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "lubridate", "patchwork"))
```

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(patchwork)
```

### Python {.unlisted}

If needed, run this once in a terminal:

```bash
python -m pip install numpy pandas matplotlib seaborn statsmodels scikit-misc
```

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import seaborn as sns
import statsmodels.api as sm
from skmisc.loess import loess

DATA_DIR = Path("data")
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")
```
:::

## Air quality in New York

When studying two numeric variables, a scatter plot is a useful starting
point. The `airquality` dataset contains daily measurements from New York
between May and September 1973.

The variables are:

- `Ozone`: mean ozone in parts per billion (ppb), measured from 1300 to 1500
  hours at Roosevelt Island.
- `Solar.R`: solar radiation in Langleys, in the frequency band 4000–7700
  Angstroms, measured from 0800 to 1200 hours at Central Park.
- `Wind`: average wind speed in miles per hour (mph), measured at 0700 and
  1000 hours at LaGuardia Airport.
- `Temp`: maximum daily temperature in degrees Fahrenheit at LaGuardia Airport.
- `Month`, `Day`: the month and day of the measurement.

The dataset is built into R. Python reads a CSV copy of the same data,
including its missing measurements. Here are the first few rows.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
head(airquality)
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
airquality = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "airquality.csv")
airquality.head()
```
:::

Let's begin with wind and ozone. If we are interested in how ozone varies
with wind speed, a natural mapping places wind speed on the x axis and ozone
on the y axis.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Wind, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Wind speed (mph)", y = "Ozone (ppb)")
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=airquality, x="Wind", y="Ozone", ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Wind speed (mph)", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

Ozone tends to decrease as wind speed increases, but the downward curvature
suggests that a straight line may be too restrictive. An inverse relationship,
such as

$$
\text{ozone} = \frac{c}{\text{wind speed}}
$$

for some constant $c$, is one possible model. The scatter plot alone does not
establish this particular form.

## Linear regression and LOESS

Scatter plots show the variation between individual days. Adding a fitted
line helps us see the average trend. We will compare two choices:

- Linear regression fits a straight line by least squares.
- LOESS fits local regressions, allowing the curve to bend.

### Adding the fits

Let's begin with the wind–ozone scatter plot. Slightly transparent points
make overlapping observations easier to see.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
ozone_wind <-
  ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Wind, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Wind speed (mph)", y = "Ozone (ppb)")

ozone_wind
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=airquality, x="Wind", y="Ozone", alpha=0.5, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Wind speed (mph)", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

We will use a dashed blue line for linear regression and a solid orange curve
for LOESS. In R, a fitted layer can be saved and reused. In Python, we define
a helper that fits both models and draws their predictions on the supplied
axes. It also returns the fitted models for the confidence-band example later.

Each fit uses the observations with both plotted variables available. Both
LOESS implementations use local quadratic fits with a span of `0.75`.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
linear_fit <- geom_smooth(
  method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
  colour = "steelblue", linetype = "dashed"
)

loess_fit <- geom_smooth(
  method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, span = 0.75, se = FALSE,
  colour = "darkorange"
)

ozone_wind + linear_fit + loess_fit
```

Here, `x` and `y` in `y ~ x` refer to the variables mapped to the axes.
`se = FALSE` hides the confidence bands while we compare the fitted trends.

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
def add_trends(x, y, data, ax, span=0.75):
    pair = data[[x, y]].dropna()
    x_grid = np.linspace(pair[x].min(), pair[x].max(), 80)

    linear_fit = sm.OLS(pair[y], sm.add_constant(pair[x])).fit()
    loess_fit = loess(
        pair[x].to_numpy(), pair[y].to_numpy(), span=span, degree=2
    )
    loess_fit.fit()

    ax.plot(
        x_grid, linear_fit.predict(sm.add_constant(x_grid)),
        color="steelblue", linestyle="--"
    )
    ax.plot(x_grid, loess_fit.predict(x_grid).values, color="darkorange")
    return x_grid, linear_fit, loess_fit


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=airquality, x="Wind", y="Ozone", alpha=0.5, ax=ax)
fitted_trends = add_trends("Wind", "Ozone", data=airquality, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Wind speed (mph)", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

`sm.add_constant()` adds the intercept to the linear model. The LOESS
prediction gives the fitted mean at each value in `x_grid`.
:::

A LOESS span of `0.75` uses roughly three quarters of the observations for
each local fit. Smaller values give more flexible curves, while larger
values give smoother curves. See the documentation for
[ggplot2 smoothing](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_smooth.html)
and [scikit-misc LOESS](https://has2k1.github.io/scikit-misc/stable/generated/skmisc.loess.loess.html).

## Comparing all six relationships

Take some time to plot the associations between `Ozone`, `Solar.R`, `Wind`,
and `Temp` and try to identify any patterns you observe.

There are six distinct pairs among these four variables. We can put the
pairs in a table and define each axis label once. This section uses functions
and iteration to avoid repeating the plotting code.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
variable_labels <- c(
  Ozone = "Ozone (ppb)",
  Solar.R = "Solar radiation\n(Langleys)",
  Wind = "Wind speed (mph)",
  Temp = "Temperature (F)"
)

plot_pairs <- tribble(
  ~x,        ~y,
  "Wind",    "Ozone",
  "Temp",    "Ozone",
  "Solar.R", "Ozone",
  "Wind",    "Temp",
  "Solar.R", "Temp",
  "Solar.R", "Wind"
)

scatter_plot <- function(x, y, data, labels) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = .data[[x]], y = .data[[y]])) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
    labs(x = labels[[x]], y = labels[[y]])
}

plot_pairs <- plot_pairs %>%
  mutate(scatter = map2(
    x, y, scatter_plot, data = airquality, labels = variable_labels
  ))

head(plot_pairs)
```

The entries in `x` and `y` are column names stored as strings.
`.data[[x]]` tells ggplot to look up the column whose name is stored in `x`;
`aes()` records this lookup and evaluates it when the plot is built.
`map2()` calls `scatter_plot()` for each pair, passing the same data and
labels each time. The resulting `scatter` column is a list of plots.

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
variable_labels = {
    "Ozone": "Ozone (ppb)",
    "Solar.R": "Solar radiation\n(Langleys)",
    "Wind": "Wind speed (mph)",
    "Temp": "Temperature (F)",
}

plot_pairs = pd.DataFrame({
    "x": ["Wind", "Temp", "Solar.R", "Wind", "Solar.R", "Solar.R"],
    "y": ["Ozone", "Ozone", "Ozone", "Temp", "Temp", "Wind"],
})


def scatter_plot(x, y, data, labels, ax):
    sns.scatterplot(data=data, x=x, y=y, alpha=0.5, ax=ax)
    ax.set(xlabel=labels[x], ylabel=labels[y])


plot_pairs.head()
```

Seaborn accepts column names as strings directly. Our helper draws each pair
on the supplied axes, using the same data and label dictionary each time.
:::

We can now arrange all six scatter plots together. R uses **patchwork** to
arrange its list of plots. Python creates six axes and loops over the rows
of the pair table.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
wrap_plots(plot_pairs$scatter, ncol = 3)
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 7))
for ax, (x, y) in zip(axes.flat, plot_pairs.itertuples(index=False, name=None)):
    scatter_plot(x, y, data=airquality, labels=variable_labels, ax=ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

Which relationships look roughly linear, and which suggest curvature?

### Adding fits to all six relationships

We can extend `scatter_plot()` with the fitted trends and reuse the same
pair table to compare all six relationships.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
trend_plot <- function(x, y, data, labels) {
  scatter_plot(x, y, data, labels) +
    linear_fit +
    loess_fit
}

plot_pairs <- plot_pairs %>%
  mutate(plot = map2(
    x, y, trend_plot, data = airquality, labels = variable_labels
  ))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
wrap_plots(plot_pairs$plot, ncol = 3)
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
def trend_plot(x, y, data, labels, ax, span=0.75):
    scatter_plot(x, y, data=data, labels=labels, ax=ax)
    return add_trends(x, y, data=data, ax=ax, span=span)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 7))
for ax, (x, y) in zip(axes.flat, plot_pairs.itertuples(index=False, name=None)):
    trend_plot(x, y, data=airquality, labels=variable_labels, ax=ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

Where does a straight line capture the main trend, and where does LOESS reveal
curvature? Which relationships still show considerable scatter? Try changing
the LOESS span to `0.5` or `1` and see which features remain visible. In R,
update `loess_fit` and rebuild the plots; in Python, pass `span=0.5` or
`span=1` to `trend_plot()`.

### Adding confidence bands

Now draw all six relationships again with confidence bands. The shading
shows 95% confidence intervals for the estimated mean trend at each x value;
the LOESS intervals are approximate. Individual days can vary much more than
the width of these bands.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

Replace the fitted layers with versions using `se = TRUE`, then reuse
`trend_plot()`. `level = 0.95` sets the confidence level.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
linear_fit <- geom_smooth(
  method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, level = 0.95,
  colour = "steelblue", fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.15,
  linetype = "dashed"
)

loess_fit <- geom_smooth(
  method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, span = 0.75, se = TRUE, level = 0.95,
  colour = "darkorange", fill = "darkorange", alpha = 0.15
)

plot_pairs <- plot_pairs %>%
  mutate(plot_with_bands = map2(
    x, y, trend_plot, data = airquality, labels = variable_labels
  ))

wrap_plots(plot_pairs$plot_with_bands, ncol = 3)
```

### Python {.unlisted}

Use the fitted models returned by `trend_plot()` to obtain intervals, then
draw the shading with `fill_between()`. The `mean_ci_lower` and
`mean_ci_upper` columns contain intervals for the mean. An `alpha` of `0.05`
gives 95% confidence intervals; the plotting `alpha=0.15` controls transparency.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 7))
for ax, (x, y) in zip(axes.flat, plot_pairs.itertuples(index=False, name=None)):
    x_grid, linear_fit, loess_fit = trend_plot(
        x, y, data=airquality, labels=variable_labels, ax=ax
    )
    linear_bands = linear_fit.get_prediction(
        sm.add_constant(x_grid)
    ).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
    loess_bands = loess_fit.predict(
        x_grid, stderror=True
    ).confidence(alpha=0.05)

    ax.fill_between(
        x_grid, linear_bands["mean_ci_lower"], linear_bands["mean_ci_upper"],
        color="steelblue", alpha=0.15
    )
    ax.fill_between(
        x_grid, loess_bands.lower, loess_bands.upper,
        color="darkorange", alpha=0.15
    )
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

See [statsmodels prediction intervals](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.regression.linear_model.OLSResults.get_prediction.html)
and [scikit-misc pointwise confidence intervals](https://has2k1.github.io/scikit-misc/stable/generated/skmisc.loess.loess_prediction.html)
for the Python methods used here.

## Longitudinal data

These data are longitudinal: measurements follow the same setting over time.
Combine the day and month into a date to examine how ozone varies through
the five months.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
airquality_formatted <-
  airquality %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(Date = make_date(1973, Month, Day))

head(airquality_formatted)
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
airquality_formatted = airquality.copy()
airquality_formatted["Date"] = pd.to_datetime({
    "year": 1973,
    "month": airquality["Month"],
    "day": airquality["Day"],
})
airquality_formatted.head()
```
:::

Here is our first attempt, using a line to show ozone over time.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 1.8
p1 <-
  ggplot(airquality_formatted, aes(Date, Ozone)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(y = "Ozone (ppb)")

p1
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3))
ax.plot(airquality_formatted["Date"], airquality_formatted["Ozone"])
ax.set(xlabel="Date", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

Why are there holes in the plot? Missing ozone values break the line. An
observed value surrounded by missing values has no line segment, so it is
invisible without a point layer.

Dropping the missing values allows the remaining observations to connect,
even when there are missing days between them.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 1.8
airquality_nona <- drop_na(airquality_formatted, Ozone)

p2 <-
  ggplot(airquality_nona, aes(Date, Ozone)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(y = "Ozone (ppb)")

p2
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
airquality_nona = airquality_formatted.dropna(subset=["Ozone"]).copy()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3))
ax.plot(airquality_nona["Date"], airquality_nona["Ozone"])
ax.set(xlabel="Date", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

Adding points shows which dates have observed measurements, although the
lines still connect across missing days.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 1.8
p3 <- p2 + geom_point()
p3
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3))
ax.plot(
    airquality_nona["Date"], airquality_nona["Ozone"],
    marker="o", markersize=3
)
ax.set(xlabel="Date", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

### Keeping gaps for missing observations

To leave gaps where measurements are missing, keep the original rows and add
points. The line breaks at missing measurements, while the points show all
observed values. In R, `na.rm = TRUE` silently omits missing points; it does
not change the data used by the line layer. Matplotlib also leaves gaps at
missing values when drawing the line.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 1.8
p_gaps <- p1 + geom_point(na.rm = TRUE)
p_gaps
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3))
ax.plot(
    airquality_formatted["Date"], airquality_formatted["Ozone"],
    marker="o", markersize=3
)
ax.set(xlabel="Date", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

Compare this with the previous plot: where did dropping missing values join
observations across missing days?

### Air pollution across the week

We might wonder whether ozone differs between weekdays and weekends. Weekly
grid lines can help us look for a repeating pattern in the time plot. They
mark weekly intervals, rather than identifying both weekend days separately.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 1.8
p4 <- p3 + scale_x_date(minor_breaks = "weeks")
p4
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3))
ax.plot(
    airquality_nona["Date"], airquality_nona["Ozone"],
    marker="o", markersize=3
)
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator())
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b"))
ax.xaxis.set_minor_locator(mdates.WeekdayLocator(byweekday=mdates.SU))
ax.grid(which="minor", axis="x", alpha=0.3)
ax.set(xlabel="Date in 1973", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

It is hard to see a clear weekly pattern because ozone varies substantially
from day to day. Let's instead create a variable representing the day of
the week.

The default R `wday()` numbering is **1 for Sunday through 7 for Saturday**.
Pandas starts at **0 for Monday through 6 for Sunday**, so we convert its
numbers to match the R example.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
airquality_1973 <-
  airquality_nona %>%
  mutate(Weekday = wday(Date))

head(airquality_1973)

ggplot(airquality_1973, aes(Weekday, Ozone)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(y = "Ozone (ppb)")
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
airquality_1973 = airquality_nona.copy()
airquality_1973["Weekday"] = (airquality_1973["Date"].dt.dayofweek + 1) % 7 + 1
airquality_1973.head()
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=airquality_1973, x="Weekday", y="Ozone", ax=ax)
ax.set(ylabel="Ozone (ppb)", xticks=range(1, 8))
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

Box plots make the distributions easier to compare. In R, converting the
weekday numbers to a factor creates separate groups for the boxes.
`as.ordered()` uses the existing numeric order; it does not discover the
calendar order. A regular factor would also create separate groups.
Python uses an ordered categorical column to make the group order explicit.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
ggplot(airquality_1973, aes(as.ordered(Weekday), Ozone)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Weekday", y = "Ozone (ppb)")
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
airquality_1973["Weekday"] = pd.Categorical(
    airquality_1973["Weekday"], categories=range(1, 8), ordered=True
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
sns.boxplot(data=airquality_1973, x="Weekday", y="Ozone", color="lightgray", ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Weekday", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

There is no clear pattern across the days of the week. Do the box plots
suggest any consistent difference between weekends and other days?

Additionally, take some time to visualize the relationships between time
and the other variables in the dataset.

### Using day names on the axis

Day names make it easier to identify weekdays and weekends. We keep Sunday
first to match the numbered plots. R's `wday(label = TRUE)` creates an ordered
factor directly; Python uses a categorical column with an explicit order.
The `"C"` locale gives English day names in both examples.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
airquality_1973_named <-
  airquality_nona %>%
  mutate(Weekday = wday(Date, label = TRUE, week_start = 7, locale = "C"))

ggplot(airquality_1973_named, aes(Weekday, Ozone)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Day of the week", y = "Ozone (ppb)")
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
weekday_order = ["Sun", "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat"]
airquality_1973_named = airquality_nona.copy()
airquality_1973_named["Weekday"] = pd.Categorical(
    airquality_1973_named["Date"].dt.day_name(locale="C").str[:3],
    categories=weekday_order, ordered=True
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
sns.boxplot(
    data=airquality_1973_named, x="Weekday", y="Ozone", color="lightgray", ax=ax
)
ax.set(xlabel="Day of the week", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

To display Monday first, set `week_start = 1` in R or move `"Sun"` to the
end of `weekday_order` in Python and recreate the categorical column. Have
the observations or box-plot summaries changed, or only the labels and order?

### Weekend and non-weekend summary

Let's compare weekends (Saturday and Sunday) with other days, using the
observed ozone measurements. The mean and median are in ppb.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
weekend_summary <-
  airquality_1973_named %>%
  mutate(DayType = if_else(Weekday %in% c("Sat", "Sun"), "Weekend", "Non-weekend")) %>%
  group_by(DayType) %>%
  summarise(
    Observations = n(),
    Mean_Ozone = round(mean(Ozone), 1),
    Median_Ozone = median(Ozone),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

weekend_summary
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
airquality_day_type = airquality_1973_named.assign(
    DayType=np.where(
        airquality_1973_named["Weekday"].isin(["Sat", "Sun"]),
        "Weekend", "Non-weekend"
    )
)
weekend_summary = (
    airquality_day_type.groupby("DayType", as_index=False)
    .agg(
        Observations=("Ozone", "size"),
        Mean_Ozone=("Ozone", "mean"),
        Median_Ozone=("Ozone", "median"),
    )
    .round({"Mean_Ozone": 1})
)
weekend_summary
```
:::

What do the means and medians support? These summaries describe the observed
days and do not adjust for weather or month.

### Comparing months

The time-series plots suggest higher ozone levels in the summer. Let's
compare monthly distributions using box plots, keeping May to September
in calendar order.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
airquality_month_named <-
  airquality_formatted %>%
  mutate(Month = factor(Month, levels = 5:9, labels = month.name[5:9]))

ggplot(airquality_month_named, aes(Month, Ozone)) +
  geom_boxplot(na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Ozone (ppb)")
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
month_order = ["May", "June", "July", "August", "September"]
airquality_month_named = airquality_formatted.copy()
airquality_month_named["Month"] = pd.Categorical(
    airquality_month_named["Date"].dt.month_name(locale="C"),
    categories=month_order, ordered=True
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
sns.boxplot(
    data=airquality_month_named, x="Month", y="Ozone", color="lightgray", ax=ax
)
ax.set(xlabel="Month", ylabel="Ozone (ppb)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

We can also count observed and missing ozone measurements in each month.
The mean and median use only observed values and are in ppb.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R {.unlisted}

```{r}
monthly_summary <-
  airquality_month_named %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarise(
    Observations = sum(!is.na(Ozone)),
    Missing = sum(is.na(Ozone)),
    Mean_Ozone = round(mean(Ozone, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Median_Ozone = median(Ozone, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

monthly_summary
```

### Python {.unlisted}

```{python}
monthly_summary = (
    airquality_month_named.groupby("Month", observed=False, as_index=False)
    .agg(
        Observations=("Ozone", "count"),
        Missing=("Ozone", lambda values: values.isna().sum()),
        Mean_Ozone=("Ozone", "mean"),
        Median_Ozone=("Ozone", "median"),
    )
    .round({"Mean_Ozone": 1})
)
monthly_summary
```
:::

Which months have higher ozone levels, and how much do their distributions
overlap? Notice that June has only nine observed values; its summary is
based on much less data.

## Source code

This paired handout follows the [R Air Quality worked example](../airquality.html).
The R dataset and Python CSV contain the same measurements, so comparisons
use the same observed days in both languages.
